# System Architecture {.unnumbered}

> Status: 🟢 Stable

---

## Two clearly separated subsystems

The system is split into two independent parts that communicate asynchronously:

1. **The weather station** — a low-power field device. Measures, stores, sleeps.
2. **The backend** — a home server that ingests, stores, and visualizes data, and runs predictive models.

These two parts are **never directly connected**. The phone acts as a physical data mule — an asynchronous gateway.

---

## Data flow overview

```{mermaid}
%%| column: page
flowchart TB
    subgraph Station["🌦️ Weather Station (ESP32)"]
        S1[Sensors] --> MCU[ESP32]
        MCU --> SD[SD Card]
        MCU -.->|"Primary: Auto Wi-Fi Client"| API
        MCU -->|"Fallback: Wi-Fi AP (SERVER mode)"| DL
    end

    subgraph Phone["📱 Phone Gateway (Fallback)"]
        DL[Download logs<br/>via browser] --> UL[Upload to server<br/>over home Wi-Fi]
    end

    subgraph Backend["🖥️ SBC Server"]
        API[REST API<br/>FastAPI]
        DB[Database<br/>InfluxDB v1]
        DASH[Dashboard<br/>TBD]
        ML[ML Models<br/>RF + LSTM]
        API --> DB --> DASH
        DB --> ML
    end

    UL -->|"Home Wi-Fi"| API
```

The station operates fully autonomously. Data is collected on the local SD card and automatically pushed to the backend server whenever the home Wi-Fi network is in range. If the station is deployed out of range, the phone acts as an offline fallback gateway to download and transfer logs manually.

---

## Station — operating principle

The station follows a **wake-do-sleep** cycle. The ESP32 spends the vast majority of its life in deep sleep, consuming microamps.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant RTC as DS3231 RTC
    participant ESP as ESP32
    participant SD as SD Card

    RTC->>ESP: Alarm interrupt (every N minutes)
    ESP->>ESP: Boot & evaluate FSM state
    ESP->>RTC: Read timestamp
    ESP->>ESP: Read all sensors
    ESP->>SD: Append CSV row
    ESP->>RTC: Set next alarm (now + interval)
    ESP->>ESP: Enter deep sleep
```

Key principle: **no code runs during deep sleep**. Every wake-up is a fresh boot.

---

## Station — finite state machine (FSM)

At every boot, the firmware evaluates the system state and executes exactly one role:

```{mermaid}
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> BOOT

    BOOT --> CHECK_WAKEUP : esp_sleep_get_wakeup_cause()

    CHECK_WAKEUP --> INIT_RTC : Power-on (UNDEFINED) AND RTC invalid
    CHECK_WAKEUP --> DATA_LOGGER : Power-on (UNDEFINED) AND RTC valid
    CHECK_WAKEUP --> DATA_LOGGER : EXT0 — RTC alarm interrupt
    CHECK_WAKEUP --> SERVER : EXT1 — button press / magnet wave

    SERVER --> INIT_RTC : Long button press (NTP sync)
    INIT_RTC --> SERVER : NTP sync successful / completed

    DATA_LOGGER --> WIFI_UPLOAD : Measurements written AND Wi-Fi available
    DATA_LOGGER --> DEEP_SLEEP : Measurements written AND Wi-Fi NOT available
    WIFI_UPLOAD --> DEEP_SLEEP : Upload complete OR timeout/error

    SERVER --> DEEP_SLEEP : 3-minute timeout OR completed manual sync

    DEEP_SLEEP --> [*]
```

At every boot, `esp_sleep_get_wakeup_cause()` is called first. Three wakeup causes are handled:

- **`UNDEFINED`** (power-on): Checks RTC validity — if invalid, go to `INIT_RTC` to perform NTP sync over Wi-Fi; if valid, go directly to `DATA_LOGGER` to take an initial measurement before sleeping.
- **`EXT0`** (RTC alarm interrupt): go directly to `DATA_LOGGER`.
- **`EXT1`** (button press / magnet wave): fires when the momentary button is pressed or magnet waved near the reed switch, waking the device to go directly to `SERVER` mode (AP mode fallback). The return to deep sleep is handled automatically in software via a 3-minute timer or upon successful sync completion.

This requires the button/reed switch to be wired to an EXT1-capable GPIO and registered as a wakeup source, which is what disambiguates a manual trigger from a scheduled alarm or fresh power-on. States are **mutually exclusive**. The FSM is deterministic and fully observable via the status LED:

### Status LED behavior

| System state | LED behavior |
|--------------|--------------|
| `DATA_LOGGER` | Off (deep sleep) |
| `WIFI_UPLOAD` | Rapid blink (250 ms) |
| `SERVER` | Steady on |
| `INIT_RTC` | Slow blink (500 ms) |
| `Critical error` | Fast blink (100 ms) |

The LED reflects **actual system state**, never user intent.

---

## Data Synchronization Strategy

Moving data from the field weather station (ESP32) to the backend server (Raspberry Pi/ODROID) involves selecting a **Trigger Mechanism** (how the station wakes up to sync) and a **Communication Medium** (how the data is transmitted). 

### 1. Our Selected Hybrid Approach
To ensure the station is both easy to use in its final outdoor location and simple to configure during the initial testing phase, the project uses a **hybrid Wi-Fi synchronization strategy**:

*   **Primary Sync — Automated Wi-Fi Client:** When deployed within range of the home Wi-Fi network, the station operates fully automatically. Once or twice a day, the ESP32 wakes up, connects as a Wi-Fi client to the home router, transmits new CSV log rows to the backend REST API (`POST /api/upload`), and goes back to sleep.
*   **Secondary Sync — Manual Wi-Fi AP (Testing & Out-of-Range Backup):** During the initial prototyping phase (when no home router is configured or available) or if the station is deployed out of Wi-Fi range, the user can manually sync the device. Waking the device via a **momentary button** (or waving a magnet near a **reed switch**) triggers the ESP32 to spin up its own Wi-Fi Access Point (`SERVER` mode) for a temporary **3-minute window**. The user connects their phone and downloads logs via a web browser. A software timer automatically returns the device to deep sleep once the window expires, protecting the battery from accidental drain.

---

### 2. Physical Trigger: Toggle Switch vs. Momentary Button
The method used to manually trigger the sync mode impacts both battery safety and enclosure waterproofing:

*   **Latching Toggle Switch:** Requires a physical toggle to be flipped to `SERVER` mode, and **must be manually flipped back** to `MEASURE` mode. 
*   **Momentary Push Button (or Magnetic Reed Switch):** Closes a circuit briefly to wake the ESP32 via a wake-up pin (`EXT0`/`EXT1`). 
    *   *Pros:* The firmware controls the sync window duration and automatically goes back to deep sleep. The user cannot accidentally drain the battery. A magnetic reed switch can be placed entirely inside the enclosure, allowing a **100% hermetically sealed** weatherproof box (zero external holes).

---

### 3. Wireless Technology: BLE vs. Wi-Fi
While consumer smart-home sensors (like SwitchBot) use Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), this project opts for Wi-Fi for direct data transfer due to the following trade-offs:

| Feature | BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) | Wi-Fi (Direct Connection) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Battery Life** | 🟢 **Excellent:** Fast transmit time (~1s), low peak current (~80mA), no router connection handshake. | 🟡 **Moderate:** Takes 3–5s to connect to the router, get an IP via DHCP, and complete TCP handshakes. Draws ~120–150mA. |
| **Bulk Data Transfer (SD Sync)** | 🔴 **Low Throughput:** BLE packet limits (typically 20–244 bytes MTU) require writing custom chunking, reassembly, and error-checking logic to transfer weeks of historical CSV logs. | 🟢 **High Throughput:** Standard TCP/IP allows the ESP32 to upload a multi-megabyte CSV file in a single, robust HTTP POST request in seconds. |
| **Protocol Simplicity** | 🔴 **Complex:** Requires designing custom GATT services/characteristics and managing async BLE scanners on the backend server. | 🟢 **Simple:** Uses standard web HTTP REST APIs and JSON payloads. Very easy to develop, test, and debug. |
| **Signal Range** | 🔴 **Shorter:** Low transmit power (1–10 mW) makes it difficult to penetrate thick exterior walls. | 🟢 **Longer:** Higher transmit power (100–200 mW) yields better range and wall-penetration. |



## Backend — server role

The Single Board Computer (SBC) acts as the home server. While the **ODROID C4** is used for prototyping (since it is already owned), a **Raspberry Pi** (such as a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W in a rugged case like the FLIRC aluminum case, or a Pi 4/5) is the preferred production choice due to lower cost, standard hardware interfaces, and wider ecosystem support.

The backend is always on and provides:
- **Data ingestion** — REST endpoint that accepts uploaded CSV batches or serial data packets
- **Storage** — time-series database (Tinyflux prototype → InfluxDB v1 or SQLite production)
- **Visualization** — web dashboard with historical data and derived metrics (Grafana or Plotly Dash)
- **Inference** — runs trained ML models to produce watering recommendations and short-term weather forecasts

---

## Key design invariants

These do not change across phases:

| Invariant | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Time authority | DS3231 RTC |
| Primary storage | SD card (append-only CSV) |
| Station-server link | Asynchronous (Wi-Fi direct or manual browser download) |
| Data format | `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,fields...` |
| Firmware model | Wake-do-sleep FSM |
| Internet at station | Never required |
::: {.callout-note}
**Data Ingestion Link:** Direct Wi-Fi upload from the station serves as the primary data path. The manual phone-based gateway remains as a valid fallback and local recovery path. Other wireless technologies (like LoRa or Cellular) are architectural alternatives but are not part of the active roadmap. See the [Data Ingestion & Fallback Gateway](#connectivity-options) section below for details.
:::

---

## Connectivity options {#connectivity-options}

The weather station implements a single primary data-path strategy: **Direct Wi-Fi Push**, with a **Phone-based Gateway** as a local manual fallback. The local SD card and its CSV log are always present and serve as the source of truth regardless of the upload method.

Other connectivity options (such as LoRa or Cellular) are documented below as alternative architectural paths that were considered for remote deployments, but they are not part of the active implementation roadmap.

---

### A — Direct Wi-Fi Push (Primary)

The ESP32 has built-in Wi-Fi hardware. During normal operation (Phase 2+), the station logs the sensor measurement to the SD card, transitions to the `WIFI_UPLOAD` state, connects to the home Wi-Fi network, and uploads the new CSV log rows to the backend REST API (`POST /api/upload`). It then immediately disconnects and enters deep sleep. No manual intervention or phone trip is required.

**How it works:**

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant RTC as DS3231 RTC
    participant ESP as ESP32
    participant SD as SD Card
    participant AP as Home Wi-Fi
    participant H as Home server

    RTC->>ESP: Alarm interrupt
    ESP->>ESP: Read sensors
    ESP->>SD: Append CSV row
    ESP->>AP: Connect (WPA2)
    ESP->>H: POST /api/upload (latest row)
    H-->>ESP: 200 OK
    ESP->>AP: Disconnect
    ESP->>ESP: Deep sleep
```

**Trade-offs:** No extra hardware cost. Dashboard updates within minutes of each measurement. Range is limited to home Wi-Fi coverage (~50–100 m). Power budget increases slightly — a Wi-Fi connect + POST + disconnect adds roughly 5–10 seconds at ~200 mA; on a 1000 mAh battery with 10-minute intervals this is still well within budget.

---

### B — Phone Gateway (Fallback / Offline / Testing)

The station has no radio link at all during normal operation when configured for offline mode or when out of Wi-Fi range. Data accumulates on the SD card. Waking the device manually via a momentary button press (or magnet wave) triggers `SERVER` mode. The ESP32 spins up its own Wi-Fi Access Point, allowing the user to connect their phone and download the CSV files via a mobile browser. These logs can later be uploaded to the backend server.

**How it works:**

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Station (SD + AP)
    participant P as Phone
    participant H as Home server

    Note over S: Days of autonomous logging
    P->>S: Connect to WeatherStation AP
    P->>S: Download log_2026.csv
    Note over P: User walks home
    P->>H: Upload CSV over home Wi-Fi
    H-->>P: 200 OK
```

**Trade-offs:** Zero infrastructure required at the station. Works anywhere — field, rooftop, or remote garden. The cost is manual effort: someone must physically visit the station to collect data, resulting in higher data latency.

---

### Alternative Connectivity Options (Not in Roadmap)

The options below were evaluated for remote deployments but are not part of the active implementation path.

#### C — LoRa (Alternative)

::: {.callout-note}
**What is LoRa?**

LoRa (**Lo**ng **Range**) is a radio modulation technique developed by Semtech. It operates on unlicensed sub-GHz ISM bands (868 MHz in Europe, 915 MHz in the US) and uses **chirp spread spectrum** to achieve exceptional range (1–15 km) at very low transmit power.

**LoRaWAN** is the network protocol built on top of LoRa radio. The Things Network (TTN) is a community-operated LoRaWAN network that allows nodes to upload data for free wherever gateway coverage exists. Alternatively, a DIY gateway costs $50–100 (Raspberry Pi + LoRa HAT).

Boards like the **Heltec WiFi LoRa32** or **TTGO LoRa32** combine an ESP32 and a SX1276 LoRa transceiver on a single board, making the hardware swap straightforward.
:::

A new `PUSH` FSM state sends a compact binary-encoded measurement packet over LoRa after each SD write. The packet is received by a LoRaWAN gateway (TTN or local), forwarded to a TTN application, and relayed to the home server via a webhook or MQTT bridge.

**How it works:**

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant ESP as ESP32 + LoRa module
    participant GW as LoRaWAN Gateway
    participant TTN as TTN Network Server
    participant H as Home server

    ESP->>GW: LoRa uplink (~50 bytes, 868 MHz)
    GW->>TTN: Forward via internet
    TTN->>H: Webhook → POST /api/upload
    H-->>TTN: 200 OK
```

**Trade-offs:** Excellent range. The best power profile of any wireless option — the transmit window is short and the module sleeps between sends. No monthly cost if TTN coverage exists. The constraint is data rate: a single measurement row must be encoded compactly (≤50 bytes).

#### D — Cellular (GSM / LTE) (Alternative)

A GSM or LTE modem module (e.g., SIM7600 for LTE, SIM800L for 2G) is connected to the ESP32 via UART. The modem is powered down between wakes via a MOSFET to eliminate standby current.

**Trade-offs:** Works anywhere with cell coverage. The cost is a monthly SIM data plan (~€5–10/month for IoT SIMs), higher peak current during connection (~500 mA), and a more complex hardware footprint.

---

### Ingestion Strategy Comparison

| Feature | Wi-Fi Push (Primary) | Phone Gateway (Fallback) | LoRa (Alternative) | Cellular (Alternative) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Range** | ~50–100 m | Walk-up only | 1–15 km | Anywhere with cell signal |
| **Data Latency** | ~1 min | Hours to days | ~2 min | ~2 min |
| **TX Current** | ~200 mA / ~5–10 s | None at station | ~100 mA / ~1–2 s | ~500 mA / ~5–15 s |
| **Monthly Cost** | 0 | 0 | 0 (TTN) | €5–10 (SIM) |
| **Extra Hardware** | None (built-in) | None | LoRa module ~$10 | GSM module ~$15–25 |
| **Infrastructure** | Home Wi-Fi in range | None at station | LoRa gateway or TTN | Cell tower in range |
| **Roadmap Status** | **Primary** | **Fallback** | Not on roadmap | Not on roadmap |

## Station Time Management

### Why an external RTC is mandatory

| Issue | ESP32 internal timer | DS3231 RTC |
|-------|----------------------|------------|
| Survives power loss | ❌ | ✅ (CR2032 backup) |
| Drift over deep sleep | High | < 2 ppm |
| Hardware wake alarm | ❌ | ✅ |
| Absolute timestamp | ❌ | ✅ |

The DS3231 is the **sole time authority** in the system. Timestamps on the SD card always come from the RTC — never from the ESP32's internal counter.

### Alarm scheduling strategy

After every measurement cycle:

```
next_alarm = RTC.now() + measurement_interval
RTC.setAlarm(next_alarm)
```

This "rolling alarm" strategy is robust: if the ESP32 crashes mid-cycle or is reset, the next boot will simply evaluate the FSM state and continue. No state machine corruption is possible.

### RTC initialization (INIT_RTC)

Triggered when `RTC.isValid() == false` or when a manual NTP resync is requested (e.g. via the web interface in `SERVER` mode):

1. Enable Wi-Fi in station mode.
2. Connect to the home Wi-Fi network (credentials stored in flash or NVS).
3. Query the NTP server (`pool.ntp.org`).
4. Set the DS3231 time via I²C.
5. Mark the RTC as valid.
6. Disable Wi-Fi.
7. Return to `SERVER` state (or proceed to deep sleep if triggered at boot).

## Station Storage & Data Format

### File format

A single append-only CSV file is stored on the micro SD card. One row is written per measurement cycle.

```
YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,TEMP,HUM,PRES,LIGHT,UV_IDX,SOIL,RAIN,WIND_SPD,WIND_DIR
```

Example row (Phase 7+, all sensors active):
```
2026-05-13 10:25:00,18.4,62.1,1013.2,12400,2.1,54.3,0.0,0.0,0
```

Unused sensor columns are written as empty or `-1` until the corresponding hardware is installed. This keeps the CSV schema stable across all phases.

### Write procedure

To minimize file corruption risks, the micro SD card is mounted and unmounted dynamically during each active log cycle:

```
Mount SD Card
Open log file (append mode)
Write CSV row
Flush file buffer
Close log file
Unmount SD Card
```

A power loss between cycles loses at most one measurement.

### Data retention

Data is never automatically deleted by the firmware. In manual `SERVER` mode, the web interface allows the user to:
- List files on the SD card.
- Download log files.
- Delete log files (user-initiated only).

---

## Fallback Server Web Interface

### What it does

When the device enters `SERVER` mode (AP fallback gateway):
- The ESP32 spins up a Wi-Fi Access Point (SSID: `WeatherStation`, password: configurable).
- A minimal HTTP server runs on port 80.
- **No measurements occur** during `SERVER` mode.

### Web interface (minimal)

| Endpoint | Action |
|----------|--------|
| `GET /` | Status page: firmware version, RTC time, SD free space |
| `GET /files` | List log files on SD card |
| `GET /download?file=X` | Download a specific log file |
| `DELETE /delete?file=X` | Delete a log file (optional / manual recovery) |
| `POST /sync-rtc` | Trigger `INIT_RTC` NTP sync sequence |

The web interface is intentionally simple and designed to render natively in any phone browser.

---

## Electrical Pull-up & Debounce Notes

### Pull-up strategy

| Signal | Pull-up |
|--------|---------|
| I²C SDA/SCL | External 4.7 kΩ to 3.3 V |
| DS3231 INT | External 10 kΩ to 3.3 V |
| Push button / Reed switch | Internal (ESP32 pull-up) |
| LED | Series 330 Ω resistor |

### Debounce

All digital inputs are debounced to prevent false triggers:
- **Buttons / Reed switch**: 20–50 ms software delay.
- **Rain gauge / anemometer pulses**: minimum inter-pulse filter (~100 ms).

## C++ Firmware Directory Structure

The suggested C++ project layout maps directly to FSM states:

```
src/
├── main.cpp              # Boot: FSM evaluation and dispatch
├── fsm/
│   ├── data_logger.cpp   # Sensor read + SD write + alarm set
│   ├── wifi_upload.cpp   # Automated Wi-Fi connect and upload
│   ├── server.cpp        # Wi-Fi AP + web server
│   └── init_rtc.cpp      # NTP sync + DS3231 set
├── drivers/
│   ├── rtc.cpp           # DS3231 abstraction
│   ├── sensors.cpp       # All sensor reads (BME280, BH1750, etc.)
│   ├── sd_logger.cpp     # SD mount/write/unmount
│   └── pulse.cpp         # Rain + wind pulse counting
└── config.h              # Pins, intervals, credentials (gitignored)
```

Adding a new sensor only requires modifying `drivers/sensors.cpp` and updating the CSV write logic in `drivers/sd_logger.cpp`.
